# Kribble: full blog text

Kribble is a childcare discovery and booking app for parents in India, launching first in Gurugram (Gurgaon). Its team physically visits and checks every daycare, preschool and playschool before listing it. Parents will be able to compare fees, plans and facilities, book anything from a single day (One-Day Daycare) to a full year, pay in the app and get daily updates from the centre. Kribble is pre-launch; parents can join the waitlist at kribblecare.com.


---

# How to compare daycares side by side: a simple scorecard
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/compare-daycares-scorecard/

The easiest way to compare daycares is to score every centre on the same short list, straight after each visit. Give each item a score from 1 to 5, multiply by how much it matters to your family, and add it up. The total won't decide for you, but it shows you clearly where each centre is strong and weak.

## Why a scorecard helps

After three or four visits, centres start to blur. Memory tends to favour whichever you saw last.

A scorecard fixes that. You judge every centre on the same things, in the same way. It also gives two parents shared words to talk it through.

If you haven't visited yet, start with our [complete checklist for choosing a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/). It explains what to look for under each heading below.

## The scorecard you can copy

Copy this table into a notes app or spreadsheet. Fill one column per centre.

| What you're scoring | Weight (1 to 3) | Centre A (1 to 5) | Centre B (1 to 5) | Centre C (1 to 5) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Safety: gates, pickup rules, first aid, clean floors | 3 | | | |
| Staff: warmth, how they talk to children, turnover | 3 | | | |
| Ratio: adults per child in your child's room | 3 | | | |
| Hygiene: toilets, nappy area, kitchen, handwashing | 2 | | | |
| Daily routine: play, rest, outdoor time | 2 | | | |
| Food: menu, who cooks, allergies handled | 2 | | | |
| Communication: updates, how they share incidents | 2 | | | |
| Location and timings: commute, hours, late pickup | 2 | | | |
| Fees: total yearly cost, refund terms | 2 | | | |
| Gut feel: would your child be happy here? | 3 | | | |

To get a total, multiply each score by its weight, then add the column. With these weights the maximum is 120.

## How to score each item

Use the same scale every time:

- **5:** clearly good, with something you saw for yourself
- **4:** good, but you only heard it, didn't see it
- **3:** fine, nothing stood out
- **2:** a concern you'd need fixed before enrolling
- **1:** a dealbreaker

The gap between 5 and 4 matters. A centre that *says* it has a pickup authorisation form is not the same as one that showed you. Score what you saw.

For ratio, count the adults and children in the room yourself. Our guide to [teacher-to-child ratios](/blog/teacher-child-ratio-guide/) explains what to look for at each age.

For fees, work out the full first-year cost, not just the monthly figure. Admission, deposits, meals and transport add up. Our [daycare fees explainer](/blog/daycare-fees-explained/) lists every component to ask about.

## Setting your own weights

The weights in the table are a starting point. Change them to suit your family. A few examples:

- If your child has a food allergy, raise food to 3.
- If you both work long hours, raise location and timings to 3.
- If budget is tight, raise fees to 3. Be honest about it.

Keep safety, staff and ratio at 3. They shape your child's day most and are hardest to fix later.

Agree on weights *before* you visit, so you can't tilt them towards a favourite.

## Dealbreakers come first

Some things should rule a centre out, whatever its total. Decide these in advance. Common ones:

- Staff couldn't tell you who is allowed to collect your child
- You weren't allowed to see the rooms your child would use
- Toilets or the nappy area were dirty during the day
- Fees or refund terms were vague and wouldn't be put in writing

Any score of 1 on a weight-3 item usually means no. Our list of [daycare red flags](/blog/daycare-red-flags/) covers more warning signs.

## How to break a tie

Two centres often end up within a few points of each other. That's normal. Here's how to decide.

1. **Compare the weight-3 rows only.** If one centre wins on safety, staff and ratio, choose it, even if the other has better facilities.
2. **Look at the gaps.** A centre with all 4s is often a safer bet than one with some 5s and a 2.
3. **Go back at a different time.** Visit at pickup time or late morning. A busy hour shows you more than a calm tour.
4. **Try a day.** Nothing beats seeing your child there. Read why a [trial day before you enrol](/blog/trial-day-before-enrolling/) is worth it.
5. **Ask your child.** Even toddlers show you something. Do they want to go back to the toy shelf, or cling to you?

Still tied? Pick the one closer to home.

## Making it work in practice

- Fill in the scorecard straight after each visit, while it's fresh.
- Add one line of notes per row. "Teacher knelt to talk to a crying child" is more useful later than a number.
- Ask the same [questions on every visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/), so your answers line up.

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to see centres' facilities, timings and fee plans side by side. That makes the first shortlist quicker. The scorecard is still worth filling in yourself after each visit.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many daycares should I compare?

Three is a good number. It gives you a sense of what's normal without becoming overwhelming. If none of the three feels right, visit two more rather than settling.

### Should both parents score separately?

Yes, if you can. Score on your own, then compare. Where your scores differ, talk about what each of you saw. Those conversations are often where the real decision gets made.

### What if the cheapest centre scores highest?

Then it may simply be the right one. Price and quality don't always move together. Check that the low fee isn't hiding extra charges, and confirm the ratio and staffing on a second visit.

# Daycares and preschools in Sectors 45 to 51 and South City, Gurgaon
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/daycare-sector-45-51-gurgaon/

Sectors 45 to 51 are among the densest clusters of daycares and preschools in Gurgaon. Kiddenz lists close to 30 centres per sector. If you live in Sector 50 or nearby, you'll have plenty of choice within a short drive. The challenge is comparing them fairly, because so many look similar from the outside.

## How many centres are there?

Here's what [Kiddenz](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram) lists for this cluster:

| Sector | Centres listed (Kiddenz) | Median annual fee (Kiddenz) |
|---|---|---|
| [Sector 51](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram/sector-51) | about 30 | about ₹1.1 lakh |
| Sector 50 | about 29 | not listed here |
| Sector 46 | about 28 | not listed here |
| Sector 45 | about 27 | not listed here |

That's well over 100 centres listed across four sectors. Directories don't catch every centre, so the real number may be higher.

For comparison, the median across all of Gurgaon on Kiddenz is about ₹55,400 a year. Sector 51's median is roughly double that.

## What fees look like here

Sector 51's median of about ₹1.1 lakh a year puts it towards the upper end of the city. Kiddenz's citywide range runs from about ₹16,000 to ₹2 lakh, so you'll still find centres well above and below the median.

A budget example nearby: a franchise preschool in Sector 41, listed on SchoolsUniverse, charges about ₹35,000 a year with about ₹5,000 for admission. It shows how much fees can vary within a few kilometres.

Fees differ for many reasons: hours, meals, ratio, space and rent. Our guide to [preschool and daycare fees in Gurgaon](/blog/preschool-fees-gurgaon/) explains what drives the price and how to work out the full first-year cost.

## Lots of choice: how to narrow it down

With 25 to 30 centres per sector, you can't visit them all. Here's a way to get from a long list to a short one.

1. **Set your radius.** Decide the furthest you'll drive twice a day. For many families, that's their own sector and the next one or two.
2. **Filter by hours.** Cross off centres whose timings don't fit your workday, including late pickup.
3. **Filter by type.** Do you need full-day daycare, a morning preschool, or both? See [preschool vs daycare](/blog/preschool-vs-daycare/).
4. **Filter by budget.** Ask for the full first-year cost before you visit, not after.
5. **Visit three or four.** Go at a busy time of day.

Then compare them on the same terms with our [side-by-side scorecard](/blog/compare-daycares-scorecard/).

## What to check on a visit

Use our [complete checklist for choosing a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) everywhere. In this cluster, a few points deserve extra care.

### Centres in houses and builder floors

You're likely to see centres in converted homes alongside purpose-fitted buildings. Both can work well. In a house, ask:

- Are stairs gated and balconies and terraces locked?
- Where is the second exit?
- Is the outdoor play area fully enclosed and shaded?
- Are the toilets child-sized and close to the play rooms?

### Drop-off on residential roads

Inner sector roads can get busy at drop-off time, with cars and vans stopping at several centres on one street.

- Is there a safe place to stop, away from moving traffic?
- Does a staff member receive children at the gate?
- If the centre offers transport, who drives and is there an attendant?

### Telling similar centres apart

When many centres offer similar facilities, look at the people and the routine.

- How do teachers speak to a child who's upset? Do they kneel and listen?
- How long have the lead teachers worked here?
- What does a normal day look like, hour by hour?
- How are incidents reported to parents? A good answer: "We call you for anything beyond a minor bump, and write every incident in a log you can see."

Use the same [questions on every visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/) so your notes line up.

## South City

South City sits next to this cluster, and many families here look across both. The same approach works: set your radius, filter by hours and budget, and visit at a busy time. Don't rule out a centre just because it's across a sector boundary. Distance on the road matters more than the sector number.

For the wider picture, read our [guide to daycare in Gurgaon](/blog/daycare-in-gurgaon-guide/).

When Kribble launches in Gurugram, you'll be able to compare centres here by location, approach, timings and fees. Every listed centre will have been visited by the Kribble team first.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many daycares are there in Sector 50, Gurgaon?

Kiddenz lists about 29 centres in Sector 50. Nearby Sector 51 has about 30, Sector 46 about 28 and Sector 45 about 27. Directories don't list every centre, so there may be more.

### What is the average daycare fee in Sector 51?

Kiddenz shows a median of about ₹1.1 lakh a year for Sector 51. That's roughly double the citywide median of about ₹55,400. Individual centres will sit above and below it, so ask each for the full first-year cost.

### With so many options, how many should I visit?

Three or four is usually enough. Filter first by distance, hours and budget, then visit at a busy time of day. Score each one on the same list straight after the visit.

### Is a more expensive centre better?

Not necessarily. A higher fee may pay for longer hours, meals or more space, or it may reflect rent. Judge the staff, ratio, safety and routine you see on the visit.

# Creche at work in India: what the law says and how to ask your employer
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/creche-at-work-india/

In India, every establishment with 50 or more employees must provide a creche facility. The rule came in with the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017, and since November 2025 it sits within the Code on Social Security, 2020. The creche can be the employer's own or a shared one nearby.

Many parents don't know this rule exists, or aren't sure how to raise it. Here's what the law says and how to ask.

## What the 2017 amendment said

The [Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017](https://www.labour.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/06/1a64517bcba2fab5650a9ff66d429080.pdf) added a new section 11A to the 1961 Act. In plain words:

- **Who:** every establishment with fifty or more employees.
- **What:** a creche facility, within a distance set by the rules.
- **How:** either a separate creche, or along with common facilities.
- **Visits:** the employer must allow the mother four visits a day to the creche, including her rest interval.
- **Telling employees:** every establishment must inform each woman, in writing and by email or other electronic means, of every benefit under the Act when she is first appointed.

The Labour Ministry's [clarification](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/the_maternity_benefit_amendment_act2017_-clarifications.pdf) noted that the creche provision took effect from 1 July 2017.

The same amendment raised paid maternity leave to up to 26 weeks for the first two children. It also allowed work from home after leave, where the job allows and both sides agree.

## What changed in 2025

On 21 November 2025, the government [brought four labour codes into force](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib2192463.pdf), rationalising 29 older central labour laws. Maternity benefits, including the creche rule, are now covered by the Code on Social Security, 2020.

According to the government's [factsheet on the Code](https://www.pib.gov.in/FactsheetDetails.aspx?id=150473):

- The creche rule still applies to establishments with 50 or more employees.
- It is described as gender-neutral, and covers all types of establishments.
- Employers can use a common creche. It can be run by government, a municipality, a private provider, an NGO, or a group of establishments pooling resources.
- The four daily visits for the mother continue.
- The factsheet also mentions a creche allowance where no creche is provided.

Detailed rules, such as the exact distance and when an allowance can replace a creche, are set separately and can change. Check the current rules for your state, or ask HR, before relying on a specific detail.

## How it works in practice

Employers meet the rule in a few different ways.

| Set-up | What it looks like | Good to check |
|---|---|---|
| On-site creche | A room or floor inside the office | Ratios, hygiene, who runs it |
| Tie-up with a nearby daycare | Reserved seats at a centre close to the office | Distance, timings, how many seats |
| Shared creche in a business park | One creche serving several companies | Waiting lists, age limits |
| Allowance | Money towards childcare, where the rules allow | How much, and whether it covers your real cost |

An on-site creche is easiest for feeding visits. A tie-up may have better facilities but needs a short trip. The same checks apply as for any daycare. Use our guide on [how to choose a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) and the [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/).

## Near the office or near home?

An office creche makes feeding visits possible and keeps your child close. But it means your child commutes with you every day. On days you work from home or travel, it may not help at all.

Our guide to daycare near home or office walks through the trade-offs.

## How to ask your employer

Keep it friendly.

1. **Check the policy first.** Look in your offer letter, HR portal or handbook for "creche" or "childcare".
2. **Ask HR in writing.** A short email works well.
3. **Ask practical questions.** Where is the creche? What ages does it take? What are the timings? Is there a waitlist? Who runs it?
4. **Ask early.** Raise it during pregnancy or early in your leave, not the week before you return.
5. **Bring colleagues in.** If several parents need it, a joint request is easier to act on.

A simple email could say:

> "I'm returning from maternity leave in March and would like to understand our creche facility. Could you share where it is, the age range, timings and how to register? Thank you."

Fathers can ask too. The government describes the requirement as gender-neutral, and HR can tell you who is eligible to use it.

## If your employer has no creche yet

Employers with fewer than 50 employees generally aren't covered by this rule. Some larger ones may still be setting things up. You'll need your own plan.

- Look at daycares near home and near the office, then compare commutes.
- Ask about flexible hours or work from home for the first months.
- Line up a backup for sick days and closures. See [backup childcare options](/blog/backup-childcare-one-day/).

Our guide to [childcare after maternity leave](/blog/childcare-after-maternity-leave/) has a full timeline.

When Kribble launches in Gurugram, you'll be able to compare verified daycares near your home or office by fees, timings and availability.

## Frequently asked questions

### Which employers must provide a creche in India?

Establishments with 50 or more employees must provide a creche facility. The rule came in through the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 and now sits within the Code on Social Security, 2020.

### Can the creche be outside the office?

Yes. The law allows a separate creche or a shared one. Employers can use a common creche, run by government, a municipality, a private provider, an NGO or a group of employers.

### How many creche visits can a mother make during work?

The law allows four visits a day to the creche, which include her normal rest interval. Ask HR how this works with your hours and team.

### Is the Maternity Benefit Act still in force?

Since 21 November 2025, its provisions have been brought into the Code on Social Security, 2020, as part of India's four labour codes. The creche and maternity leave rights continue under the Code.

# Montessori, play-way, Reggio Emilia or traditional: preschool approaches explained
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/montessori-vs-playway-vs-reggio/

Montessori classrooms let children choose their own work with special hands-on materials, often in mixed-age groups. Play-way preschools teach through games, songs, stories and group activities led by the teacher. Reggio Emilia builds long projects around children's own questions, while traditional preschools follow a fixed, teacher-led syllabus.

No approach suits every child. What matters most is how well a centre actually practises what it claims.

## The approaches at a glance

| | Montessori | Play-way | Reggio Emilia | Traditional |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Who leads | Child chooses, teacher guides | Teacher plans playful activities | Child's interests shape projects | Teacher leads |
| Group setup | Often mixed ages | Same-age class | Small groups, often same age | Same-age class |
| Typical day | Long work period with materials | Songs, games, stories, art | Open-ended projects over days or weeks | Lessons, practice, rhymes |
| Materials | Specific Montessori materials | Toys, puzzles, art supplies | Natural and art materials, studio space | Books, worksheets, charts |
| Suits children who | Like to focus alone and work at their own pace | Enjoy group fun and variety | Are curious and love making things | Do well with clear structure |

## Montessori

Maria Montessori, an Italian physician and educator, opened her first school in Rome in 1907, [according to The Hechinger Report](https://hechingerreport.org/will-the-real-montessori-please-stand-up/). The approach centres on letting children choose activities and work at their own pace.

### What you'd see in the classroom

- Low, open shelves with neatly arranged materials
- Children working alone or in pairs, often on small mats or at low tables
- Wooden materials for practical life skills (pouring, buttoning, sweeping) and the senses
- Mixed ages in one room, often spanning about three years
- A long, uninterrupted work period, with the teacher observing and guiding quietly

### Real or just the name?

The same Hechinger report notes that "Montessori" is not a trademarked name. Any centre can use it. Ask:

- What Montessori training do your teachers have, and from which training body?
- How long is the uninterrupted work period each day?
- Can I see the materials in use, not just on shelves?
- Are the age groups mixed?

A classroom with Montessori materials on display but children doing worksheets at desks is Montessori in name only.

## Play-way

Play-way is a common label in Indian preschools for learning through play. It is a broad description, not one formal method.

### What you'd see in the classroom

- Circle time with songs, rhymes and movement
- Teacher-led games that teach colours, shapes, numbers and sounds
- Story sessions, puppets, role play and art
- Activity corners with blocks, puzzles and pretend play
- Lots of group activities, usually with children of the same age

### Real or just the name?

Because "play-way" has no fixed definition, look at what children actually do. Ask:

- How much of the day is free play versus teacher-led activity?
- Can I see this week's activity plan?
- Do children do worksheets, and from what age?

If most of the day is spent at desks copying letters, it isn't really play-based.

## Reggio Emilia

The approach grew from preschools in the Italian town of Reggio Emilia after World War II. Educator Loris Malaguzzi shaped it, [according to EBSCO's overview](https://ebsco.com/research-starters/education/reggio-emilia-approach). It sees children as capable, curious learners.

### What you'd see in the classroom

- Projects that grow from children's questions, sometimes lasting weeks
- An art studio or making space with paint, clay, light and natural materials
- Walls covered in photos, notes and children's work showing how a project developed
- A carefully arranged room, sometimes called the "third teacher"
- Children expressing ideas through drawing, building, drama and talk

### Real or just the name?

Reggio-inspired centres vary a lot. Ask:

- Can you show me a recent project and how it started?
- How do you record children's learning?
- How do children's ideas change what you plan?

## Traditional

A traditional preschool follows a set syllabus, often building towards formal school. The teacher leads, and the class moves through topics together.

### What you'd see in the classroom

- Children seated in rows or groups facing the teacher
- Letters, numbers and rhymes taught through repetition
- Worksheets, workbooks and homework
- A fixed timetable of subjects

Clear structure suits some children. But for under-fives, too much sitting, copying and testing can crowd out play, which is how young children learn best. Our guide to what good early learning looks like explains why.

## Many centres mix approaches

In practice, many Indian preschools blend these. You might see a Montessori corner, play-way circle time and a few worksheets in the same week.

That isn't a problem. Ask the centre to describe a typical day in plain words, then check it matches what you see.

## How to choose

Think about your child first. A child who loves quiet focus may thrive with Montessori. A social child may love play-way group time. A curious maker may enjoy a Reggio-inspired room.

Take our [questions to ask on a visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/) with you. Then look at the basics that matter whatever the label: warm, trained staff, a sensible ratio, safety and good communication. Our [complete guide to choosing a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) covers these. If you're still deciding between types of centre, read [preschool vs daycare vs playschool](/blog/preschool-vs-daycare/).

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to compare verified centres in Gurugram by approach, alongside fees and facilities.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Montessori better than play-way?

Neither is better for every child. Montessori suits children who like to focus and work independently, while play-way suits children who enjoy group activities and variety. The quality of the teachers matters more than the label.

### How do I know if a preschool is really Montessori?

Ask about teachers' Montessori training, the length of the daily work period and whether ages are mixed. Watch whether children are actually using the materials. The name isn't trademarked, so any centre can use it.

### What does Reggio-inspired mean?

It means a centre draws on ideas from the Reggio Emilia preschools in Italy, such as projects led by children's interests and careful documentation. It is an inspiration rather than a certification, so practice varies from centre to centre.

### Are worksheets bad for preschoolers?

A few, used lightly for older preschoolers, are not harmful. But young children learn mainly through play, talk and hands-on activity. A preschool that relies heavily on worksheets for toddlers is missing what they need most.

# Daycares and preschools on Golf Course Extension and Sohna Road
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/daycare-golf-course-extension-sohna-road/

Golf Course Extension and Sohna Road are full of newer high-rise societies. Many have a daycare inside the complex or just outside the gate. That's convenient, but convenience isn't the same as quality. Check each one as carefully as you would a centre across town, and plan around the traffic.

## Who this area suits

These corridors have grown quickly, with large gated societies and plenty of young families. Many parents work in Cyber City, on Golf Course Road or further afield, and commute daily.

For a family here, the choice often comes down to three options:

- A daycare inside your own society
- A centre in a nearby sector or on the main road
- A centre near one parent's office

Each has trade-offs. Our guide to daycare near home or near office helps you weigh them.

## What fees look like

We don't have a published median for Golf Course Extension or Sohna Road specifically. Across Gurgaon (officially Gurugram), [Kiddenz's listings](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram) show a median of about ₹55,400 a year, ranging from roughly ₹16,000 to ₹2 lakh.

For a local reference point, Kiddenz shows a median of about ₹1.1 lakh a year in [Sector 51](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram/sector-51). Our guide to [Sectors 45 to 51 and South City](/blog/daycare-sector-45-51-gurgaon/) covers that cluster in detail.

Society daycares and main-road centres can price very differently. Ask every centre for the full first-year cost in writing. Our guide to [preschool and daycare fees in Gurgaon](/blog/preschool-fees-gurgaon/) explains what to add up.

## Society daycares: what to check

A daycare a lift ride away is a real gift on busy mornings. But being inside a gated complex doesn't make a centre safe by default. Ask:

- **Who runs it?** The society, a resident, or an outside operator renting the space?
- **Who staffs it, and are they background-checked?** Ask to see the policy.
- **How is the entrance controlled?** Society security at the main gate is not the same as a locked daycare door.
- **Who can collect your child?** Ask to see the pickup authorisation form.
- **What happens in holidays?** Some society daycares close or run short staffed during festivals and summer.
- **What's the backup if the main caregiver is ill?**

A good answer is specific. "Two trained caregivers are always on site, and a third covers leave. Only names on your form can collect your child, with photo ID."

Our [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/) has the full list.

## Newer centres: what to check

Many centres here have opened in the last few years. New can be great: fresh spaces, modern equipment. It also means less track record.

- **How long has the centre been open?** And how long have the lead teachers been there?
- **Is the building finished?** Check for open construction, loose fittings or unfenced areas nearby.
- **Is the outdoor space ready and enclosed?**
- **Can you speak to a current parent?** A confident centre will usually offer.
- **Are policies in writing?** Sick policy, fee refunds, incident reporting.

Our list of [daycare red flags](/blog/daycare-red-flags/) covers warning signs to watch for.

## Traffic and the daily drive

Traffic on these corridors can be heavy at peak hours. A centre that looks close on the map can mean a long, stressful drive.

- **Try the route at drop-off time**, with your child in the car if you can.
- **Avoid U-turn traps.** A centre on the wrong side of a main road can add real time.
- **Ask about transport.** Who drives, is there an attendant, and how long is the longest ride?
- **Plan for sick days.** Who can reach the centre quickly at midday?

Often a slightly less impressive centre inside your society beats a better-looking one across a busy road. Weigh it honestly.

## Hours for working parents

Many families here need full-day care. Ask:

- What are the earliest drop-off and latest pickup times?
- How is late pickup charged?
- Is there a half-day option for work-from-home days?
- Do they offer after-school care for older siblings?

## A quick plan

1. Visit your society daycare first. It's the easiest to compare against.
2. Add two or three centres within a short drive.
3. Use the same [questions on every visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/).
4. Follow our [complete checklist for choosing a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/).
5. Do a trial day before you enrol.

For the wider picture across the city, read our [guide to daycare in Gurgaon](/blog/daycare-in-gurgaon-guide/).

When Kribble launches, every listed centre will have been visited and checked by the Kribble team first. You'll be able to compare timings, fees and real photos side by side.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a daycare inside my society safer?

Not automatically. Society gate security helps, but check the daycare's own entrance, pickup rules, staffing and background checks. Treat it like any other centre on your shortlist.

### What are daycare fees like on Sohna Road?

We don't have a published median for Sohna Road itself. Citywide, Kiddenz shows a median of about ₹55,400 a year, and nearby Sector 51 shows about ₹1.1 lakh. Ask each centre for the full first-year cost.

### How do I judge a daycare that's only just opened?

Look at the people more than the building. Ask how experienced the lead teachers are, read the written policies and ask to speak to a current parent. A trial day tells you a lot.

### What if my society daycare closes in the holidays?

Ask about holiday dates before you enrol, and plan backup care early. Options include family, a nearby centre that takes children for single days, or a holiday camp. Our guide to [backup childcare](/blog/backup-childcare-one-day/) has ideas.

# Screen time for under-5s: what the guidelines say
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/screen-time-under-5/

The World Health Organization's 2019 guidelines say screen time is not recommended for babies under 1 or for 1-year-olds. For children aged 2 to 4, sedentary screen time should be no more than one hour a day, and less is better. The guidance sits inside a bigger picture: move more, sit less and sleep well.

Here is what that means in a real home, and what to ask your daycare.

## What the WHO guidelines actually say

In April 2019, the WHO published its [guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-04-2019-to-grow-up-healthy-children-need-to-sit-less-and-play-more). Screen time is one part of it.

| Age | Sedentary screen time | Physical activity | Sleep (including naps) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Under 1 | Not recommended | Active several times a day; at least 30 minutes of tummy time for babies not yet mobile | 14 to 17 hours (0 to 3 months); 12 to 16 hours (4 to 11 months) |
| 1 year | Not recommended | At least 180 minutes a day, any intensity | 11 to 14 hours |
| 2 years | No more than 1 hour; less is better | At least 180 minutes a day, any intensity | 11 to 14 hours |
| 3 to 4 years | No more than 1 hour; less is better | At least 180 minutes, with at least 60 minutes moderate to vigorous | 10 to 13 hours |

The guidelines also say young children should not be restrained for more than an hour at a time, in a pram, high chair or carrier. When children are sitting still, reading and storytelling with a caregiver is encouraged.

### What "sedentary screen time" means

The WHO gives examples: watching TV or videos and playing computer games. It is time spent sitting and watching, rather than moving, talking or playing.

The key word is the trade-off. An hour on a screen is an hour not spent climbing, chatting, building or napping.

## Why the guidelines focus on the whole day

The guidance is not only about screens being bad. It is about what young children need more of: movement, sleep and time with people who talk and play with them.

That framing helps. Instead of a daily battle over the tablet, you can ask a simpler question. Did my child move a lot, sleep enough and have plenty of back-and-forth with an adult today?

## Making it work at home

Few families hit every target every day. Aim for the direction, not perfection.

### Practical swaps

- **Mealtimes without screens.** Talk about the food, the colours, the day.
- **A basket instead of the phone.** Keep a small box of books, blocks and crayons near where you work or cook.
- **Audio over video.** Songs and stories you listen to together keep hands and bodies free.
- **Screens off before bed.** A calm wind-down with a book suits the sleep targets better.
- **Watch together when you do watch.** Talk about what is on screen. It turns watching into a conversation.

### When you need a break

Every parent has moments when a screen buys ten quiet minutes. That is real life. If a screen helps on a hard day, choose something slow-paced and keep it short.

Sudden switch-offs can trigger tears. A warning ("Two more minutes, then we're having bath") makes the transition easier. Our guide to [toddler meltdowns](/blog/toddler-meltdowns-what-helps/) has more on handling those moments.

## Screen time at daycare and preschool

Your child may spend most waking hours at a centre, so its screen policy matters as much as yours.

Some centres use TVs for rhymes or to settle children before pickup. Others use none. Neither is automatically a red flag, but you should know what happens and why.

### Questions to ask

Add these to your [questions to ask on a daycare visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/):

- "Do children watch screens here? For how long, and when?"
- "Is it different for under-2s?" A good answer: "We don't use screens with babies and toddlers."
- "What do children do in the last hour before pickup?" This is when screens often creep in.
- "Do you use tablets for learning?" Ask what children actually do on them, and for how long.
- "How much outdoor or active play do they get each day?"

A thoughtful answer sounds specific. "We play rhymes on a speaker and sing along, but we don't use a TV" tells you more than "very little screen time".

Good early learning is hands-on. Our guide to what good early learning looks like explains what to look for in the classroom instead.

Screen policy is one line on a longer list. Our [daycare checklist](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) covers the rest, from safety to food.

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to compare centres' approach and facilities side by side before you visit.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much screen time is okay for a 2-year-old?

The WHO's 2019 guidelines say sedentary screen time for 2-year-olds should be no more than one hour a day, and less is better. The same limit applies to children aged 3 and 4. The guidelines encourage reading and storytelling with a caregiver instead.

### Is any screen time okay for babies under 1?

The WHO guidelines say screen time is not recommended for infants under 1, or for 1-year-olds. They suggest babies be active several times a day, including tummy time, and get plenty of sleep.

### Should my child's daycare use TV or tablets?

Policies vary between centres, so ask directly. Find out how long screens are used, at what times of day, and whether under-2s are included. Plenty of active play and talk with carers is what you want to hear about.

### What can I do instead of screens with a toddler?

Books, songs, simple building toys, crayons and outdoor play all work well. Audio stories and music keep children engaged without a screen. Including your child in everyday tasks, like sorting laundry, also counts as play.

# Parent communication for preschools: daily updates parents actually value
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/preschool-parent-communication/

Good preschool parent communication is short, regular and specific. Parents want to know their child ate, slept, was safe and had a good day. They want to hear about any problem from you first. A few honest lines and one good photo usually matter more than a polished newsletter.

Here is what to share, how often, and how to keep it manageable for your staff.

## What parents actually want to know

Parents of young children are handing over the most important part of their day. What they want is reassurance and a window into their child's life.

Our parent-facing guide on daily updates from daycare tells families to expect these basics:

- **Meals**: what was eaten, roughly how much, anything refused.
- **Sleep**: nap times and length.
- **Nappies or toilet visits** for younger children.
- **Mood**: settled, tired, unusually quiet, a hard drop-off.
- **Activities**: what they did, and something they enjoyed.
- **Incidents**: any bump, fall, bite or illness, however small.

If your updates already cover these, you are meeting expectations. The difference between good and great is in the detail.

## Specific beats generic

Compare two example updates:

> "Aarav had a good day."

> "Aarav ate all his dal-rice, napped for an hour and a half, and spent ages at the water table pouring between cups."

The second takes 30 seconds longer to write. It tells the parent someone actually noticed their child. It also gives them something to talk about at home.

## How often to communicate

| What | How often | Format |
|---|---|---|
| Meals, sleep, nappies, mood | Daily | Short log or app entry |
| One photo or short note on an activity | Daily or a few times a week | Photo with a line of context |
| Incident reports | The same day, before pickup | Written report plus a call for anything significant |
| What the class is learning | Weekly | A short note or plan |
| Individual progress | Each term | Observation notes and examples of work |
| Policy or fee changes | As they happen, with notice | Written notice |

Consistency matters more than volume. Parents relax when updates arrive at the same time each day.

### Extra care during settling in

The first two weeks are the hardest for families. A quick message mid-morning ("She stopped crying ten minutes after you left and is now playing with blocks") can transform a parent's day. Our guide to [settling in at daycare](/blog/settling-in-at-daycare/) shows what parents are going through.

## Photos and consent

Photos are often the part parents love most. They also need the most care.

- **Ask for written consent** at enrolment, with clear options: photos shared privately with the family, group photos, use on social media or not at all.
- **Respect the choice of every family.** In group photos, avoid showing children whose parents have not agreed.
- **Use staff-owned or centre devices with care.** Set a clear rule about where photos are stored and when they are deleted.
- **Never post identifiable photos publicly** without explicit permission.

Parents who ask about [CCTV in daycare](/blog/cctv-in-daycare/) often have similar privacy concerns. Have a clear, written answer ready for both.

## Reporting incidents well

How you handle a scraped knee affects trust more than any brochure. A good incident report:

1. **Tells the parent the same day**, before or at pickup, not days later.
2. **Says what happened, when, and where**, in plain words.
3. **Explains what staff did**: first aid, comfort, observation.
4. **Notes any follow-up**: watching for symptoms, a change to supervision.
5. **Is signed** by the staff member and acknowledged by the parent.

For anything beyond a minor bump, call the parent straight away. Then follow up in writing.

If two children are involved, such as a bite, tell both families. Do not name the other child.

## Choosing a communication tool

Many centres start with WhatsApp groups. They are easy, but they mix chatter with important messages, share every parent's number with the group and make individual updates hard to find later.

When choosing any tool, ask:

- Can each family get private updates about their own child?
- Can staff post quickly, during a busy day, on a centre device?
- Are photos shared only with the right families?
- Can parents find past updates, receipts and notices easily?
- Can you control who has access when a staff member leaves?

Kribble will give partner centres one feed to send photos, updates and notes to parents, alongside enquiries and fee collection.

## Communication as admissions

Families who feel informed tend to tell their friends. Good daily updates are one of the most effective ways to [get more preschool admissions](/blog/get-more-preschool-admissions/) through referrals.

They also answer what new parents check for when they [choose a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/): will I know what happens to my child each day?

## Frequently asked questions

### How often should a preschool update parents?

Daily updates on meals, sleep, mood and activities work well for most families, especially for younger children. Add a weekly note on what the class is learning and termly progress notes. Incidents should always be reported the same day.

### What should be in a daily daycare report?

Include meals, naps, nappies or toilet visits, mood and the main activities. A specific line about something the child enjoyed makes a big difference. Note any incident, however minor.

### Do preschools need parent consent for photos?

Asking for written consent at enrolment is good practice. Give families clear choices about private sharing, group photos and social media. Respect each family's choice in every photo you share.

### Is WhatsApp good enough for parent communication?

It is easy to start with but has drawbacks. Group chats expose parents' numbers, mix casual messages with important ones and make individual updates hard to find. A tool with private, per-child updates is usually easier to manage as you grow.

# Teacher-to-child ratio in daycares and preschools: what is good?
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/teacher-child-ratio-guide/

A good teacher-to-child ratio depends on age: the younger the child, the fewer children each adult should look after. India's National ECCE Policy 2013 sets one adult for every 10 children under 3 and one for every 20 aged 3 to 6. For babies and toddlers, many parents look for far fewer children per adult than that.

Here is why ratio matters, what the numbers look like, and how to check the real ratio on a visit.

## What a ratio means

The ratio is the number of children each adult is responsible for at one time. A 1:5 ratio means one adult for every five children.

It is different from group size, which is the total number of children in a room. A room of 20 toddlers with four adults has a 1:5 ratio, but it can still feel loud and busy. Ask about both.

## Why ratio matters more for younger children

Babies need one-to-one attention for almost everything: feeding, changing, settling to sleep and comfort when upset. An adult can only hold, feed or change one baby at a time.

Toddlers are mobile, curious and quick. They climb, put things in their mouths and test limits. They need close supervision and a lot of help with routines.

Older preschoolers can play in groups, follow instructions and manage more of their own needs. One adult can reasonably look after more of them.

In every age group, a better ratio means more conversation, more comfort and more chance someone notices when something is wrong.

## What India's ECCE policy says

India's National Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) Policy was notified in 2013. Its quality standards include these adult-to-child ratios, [as summarised by Factly](https://factly.in/quality-standards-place-play-schools-pre-schools):

| Age group | Ratio in the National ECCE Policy 2013 |
|---|---|
| Under 3 | 1 adult : 10 children |
| 3 to 6 | 1 adult : 20 children |

The same summary notes that children should never be left unattended. Treat these as a baseline, not a target.

## How international norms compare for babies

Some countries set much tighter ratios for the youngest children. England's early years framework, for example, sets these for nurseries, [as summarised here](https://www.pembee.app/blog/staff-to-child-ratios-uk):

| Age group | England's group-setting ratio |
|---|---|
| Under 2 | 1 : 3 |
| 2 years | 1 : 5 |
| 3 and over | 1 : 8, or 1 : 13 with a qualified teacher working directly with the children |

These rules don't apply in India. They are useful as a reference point for what tight infant care looks like.

## A practical guide for Indian parents

Putting this together, here is a sensible way to think about ratios when you visit:

| Your child's age | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Under 1 | As few babies per adult as possible. Ask how many babies each caregiver looks after at feeding and nap times. |
| 1 to 2 | Small groups, with one adult never stretched across a large group of toddlers. |
| 2 to 3 | Smaller groups than the older classes, with extra help at meals and toilet times. |
| 3 to 6 | At least the ECCE baseline, with a teacher plus a helper in larger classes. |

These are not rules. They are a way to judge whether what you see feels right for your child's age.

## How to check the real ratio on a visit

Centres sometimes quote a ratio that includes the principal, office staff or cooks. What matters is the number of adults caring for children in each room.

1. **Ask the ratio for your child's group, not the centre overall.** "How many children and how many adults are in the toddler room?"
2. **Count for yourself.** During your visit, count the adults actually with the children in each room.
3. **Ask who covers breaks and leave.** If a caregiver is on lunch or sick, who steps in? A good answer names a floating staff member.
4. **Ask about the busiest times.** Ratios often slip at drop-off, pickup, meals and nap time. Ask how they manage those moments.
5. **Ask whether helpers are counted.** Helpers matter, but you want to know how many trained caregivers there are.
6. **Visit at different times.** If you can, drop in once in the morning and once near pickup.

Add these to your list of [questions to ask on a daycare visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/).

## Ratio is not everything

A good ratio with unkind or untrained staff is still poor care. A slightly higher ratio with warm, experienced, consistent caregivers can work well, especially for older children.

Look at ratio alongside staff training, turnover, routine and the points in our [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/). Our [complete guide to choosing a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) covers all of these. If a room looks chaotic or children are left waiting with no adult nearby, see our list of [daycare red flags](/blog/daycare-red-flags/).

Kribble's team physically visits and checks every centre before listing it. When the app launches, you'll be able to compare centres on safety details and facilities.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a good teacher-to-child ratio for a toddler?

India's National ECCE Policy 2013 sets one adult for every 10 children under 3. Many parents prefer smaller groups than that for toddlers, who need close supervision. Count the adults in the room during your visit and ask how they manage meal and nap times.

### What is the ratio for preschool in India?

The National ECCE Policy 2013 sets one adult for every 20 children aged 3 to 6. Many preschools have a teacher plus a helper in each class, which improves this. Ask each centre for the numbers in your child's class.

### Does the ratio include helpers and nannies?

Some centres count helpers, and some don't. Helpers make a real difference, but ask how many trained caregivers are in the room as well. Ask directly so you know what the quoted number means.

### What if a centre's ratio looks worse than it said?

Ask about it calmly. There may be a reason, such as a staff break. If the gap is large or happens often, treat it as a warning sign about staffing.

# Daycares and preschools on Golf Course Road and DLF Phases 1 to 5
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/daycare-golf-course-road-dlf/

Looking for daycare on Golf Course Road or in DLF Phases 1 to 5? You'll find plenty of choice close to Cyber City. The harder part is matching hours, drop-off logistics and fees to your family. Shortlist by your daily route first, then visit at least three centres.

## Who this area suits

Golf Course Road and the DLF phases are among Gurugram's older, established neighbourhoods. The housing mix is wide: independent houses and builder floors in the DLF phases, and high-rise societies along Golf Course Road.

Many parents here work in Cyber City, Udyog Vihar or the offices along Golf Course Road itself. That makes a short commute between home, centre and office realistic. It also means centres here see a lot of full-day, dual-working-parent families.

## What fees look like

We don't have a published median for these neighbourhoods specifically. We do know the citywide picture from [Kiddenz's Gurgaon listings](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram). The median is about ₹55,400 a year, ranging from roughly ₹16,000 to ₹2 lakh.

Location moves fees a lot. On Kiddenz, [Sector 51](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram/sector-51) has a median of about ₹1.1 lakh, while Sector 92 sits at about ₹32,400. Established, central areas tend to have higher rents, so don't be surprised by quotes towards the upper end of the city range. But ask every centre rather than assuming.

Always ask for the full first-year cost: admission, deposit, meals, transport and late pickup. Our guide to [preschool and daycare fees in Gurgaon](/blog/preschool-fees-gurgaon/) shows how to add it up.

## Types of centres you'll see

You'll meet most kinds of centre here:

- **Centres in houses or builder floors**, common in the DLF phases
- **Chains and franchises**, often in purpose-fitted buildings
- **Daycares inside or beside high-rise societies**
- **Workplace creches** linked to some offices nearby

Each can be good. Judge the room your child will use and the adults in it.

## The commute to Cyber City and beyond

Being close to the office hubs is the big advantage here. Use it well.

- **Drive the route at the real time.** A short distance can still be a slow drive at rush hour.
- **Check the drop-off point.** Inner roads in the DLF phases can be narrow. Is there somewhere safe to stop, or will you double-park every morning?
- **Plan the sick-day dash.** If the centre calls at noon, who can get there in 20 minutes?
- **Ask about the latest pickup time** and the late fee, in writing.

Not sure whether to choose near home or near work? Our guide to daycare near home or near office walks through it.

## What to check in this area

Use our [complete checklist for choosing a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) on every visit. In this area, give extra attention to a few things.

### Centres in houses and builder floors

Many good centres run from converted homes. Ask to see every room your child will use, not just the reception.

- How are stairs gated? Are balconies and terraces locked or fenced?
- Where is the second exit if there's a fire?
- Where do children play outdoors, and is it fully enclosed?
- How is the kitchen kept separate from play areas?

### Society daycares

A daycare inside your society is very convenient. Check the basics anyway.

- Who runs it: the society, a resident or an outside operator?
- Does it stay open during school holidays and festivals?
- Who covers when a caregiver is ill?
- Are staff background-checked, and can you see the policy?

Our [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/) has more on what to ask.

### Hours and staffing for long days

Full-day care from early morning to evening is common here. Ask how the day is staffed.

- Do the same teachers stay all day, or is there a later shift?
- What is the ratio in the late afternoon, when some children have gone home?
- What do children do in the last hour? A good answer is calm and specific: "Free play and stories in the quiet room, with a snack at 5."

Our guide to [teacher-to-child ratios](/blog/teacher-child-ratio-guide/) explains what to look for at each age.

## A quick plan

1. Choose a radius around the parent who does most pickups.
2. Shortlist five or six centres in that radius.
3. Visit three at a busy time, using the same [questions on every visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/).
4. Confirm fees and refund terms in writing.
5. Do a trial day before you commit.

For the wider picture across the city, see our [guide to daycare in Gurgaon](/blog/daycare-in-gurgaon-guide/).

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to compare centres here on location, timings, fees and real photos. Every listed centre will have been visited by the Kribble team.

## Frequently asked questions

### Are daycares on Golf Course Road expensive?

Fees vary widely, and we don't have a published median for Golf Course Road itself. Citywide, Kiddenz shows a median of about ₹55,400 a year and a range up to about ₹2 lakh. Central areas often sit higher in that range, so ask each centre for the full first-year cost.

### Is a daycare in a house safe?

It can be, if it's set up well. Check stair gates, locked balconies and terraces, a clear second exit and an enclosed outdoor space. Ask to see every room your child will use.

### Should I pick a daycare near Cyber City or near home?

If one parent does both trips and works on a fixed schedule, near the office can work well. If you work from home some days or share pickups, near home is usually easier. Think about who reaches the centre fastest on a sick day.

### Do offices near Golf Course Road have creches?

Some employers run or partner with creches, but it varies by company. Ask your HR team what's available, the age range and how long the waitlist is. Our guide to [creche at work in India](/blog/creche-at-work-india/) has more.

# CCTV in daycare: what it can and can't tell you
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/cctv-in-daycare/

CCTV in a daycare can show you what happened in a room after the fact, and sometimes what is happening right now. It cannot tell you whether the staff are kind, attentive or well trained. Treat cameras as one useful tool, not as proof that a centre is safe.

Many parents ask about CCTV first. That makes sense. It feels like control when you're handing your child to strangers. But the questions behind the camera matter more than the camera itself.

## Live feeds vs recorded footage

There are two very different set-ups, and centres often blur them.

| | Recorded CCTV only | Live feed for parents |
|---|---|---|
| Who watches | Centre staff, usually after an incident | You, on your phone, during the day |
| Main use | Checking what happened | Reassurance, a glimpse of your child |
| Privacy risk | Lower, if access is controlled | Higher: other children are visible too |
| What to ask | How long is it kept? Who can review it? | Who else can log in? Can it be recorded or shared? |

Recorded footage is useful when something goes wrong. If your child comes home with a bump, the centre can check what happened. That only works if the cameras cover the right rooms and the footage is kept long enough.

Live feeds are a different thing. They can be lovely on a hard first week. They can also become a source of worry, as you watch a crying child and can't do anything.

## Questions to ask about CCTV

On your visit, go past "Do you have CCTV?" and ask these:

1. **Which areas are covered?** Classrooms, play areas, entrance, corridors? A good centre covers shared spaces and the entrance.
2. **What about changing and toilet areas?** These should not be filmed. Ask how those areas are supervised instead, for example with open doors or two adults present.
3. **How long is footage kept?** Ask for a number of days. If they can't tell you, the system may not be well managed.
4. **Who can view the footage?** It should be a small number of named people, not anyone in the office.
5. **Can parents see footage after an incident?** Ask how they handle this. A careful answer will balance your right to know with other children's privacy.
6. **Is anyone actually watching?** A camera nobody looks at is mostly a deterrent. Ask whether the owner or a supervisor reviews footage regularly.
7. **Are the cameras working today?** It's fair to ask to see the monitor. A dark screen or a dummy camera tells you something.

## The privacy of other children

Every live feed shows other people's children too. Some parents are fine with that. Others are not, and they have good reasons.

A thoughtful centre will have a clear policy. Who can log in? Is access removed when a family leaves? Are parents told not to record or share clips? If a centre streams to anyone who asks, your child is on screen for those people too.

## What CCTV can't tell you

Cameras can't hear tone of voice. They usually can't show how a teacher comforts a crying toddler. They can't tell you whether staff are trained, rested or paid enough to stay.

They also can't prevent harm. They record it. What prevents harm is the right number of adults per child, careful hiring and a culture where staff speak up. Our [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/) puts CCTV in its place among 20 other checks.

## Better signals than a camera

If you want to know how your child's day really goes, these tell you more:

- **The ratio in the room.** Count adults and children yourself. See our guide to [teacher-to-child ratios](/blog/teacher-child-ratio-guide/).
- **How staff talk to children.** Kneeling down, using names, calm voices. You'll see this in ten minutes of a visit.
- **Daily updates.** A short note on meals, naps and mood tells you more than hours of video. Here's what daily updates to expect.
- **A trial day.** Watching your child in the setting is worth more than any feed. Read [why a trial day helps](/blog/trial-day-before-enrolling/).
- **Your child's behaviour over time.** Settling takes a while, but a child who stays anxious for weeks is telling you something.

## So should CCTV decide where you enrol?

It can be a tie-breaker between two good centres. It should never be the reason you choose a weaker one. A centre with cameras and too few staff is a worse choice than a well-staffed centre without a live feed.

For the full picture of what to weigh, start with our guide on [how to choose a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/).

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to see safety details for each centre its team has visited. That helps you ask better questions before you go.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is CCTV compulsory in daycares in India?

Rules on childcare centres differ by state and type of centre, so check locally rather than assume. Whatever the rule, ask the centre which areas are covered and who can view the footage.

### Should daycares have cameras in changing areas?

Changing and toilet areas should not be filmed, to protect children's privacy. Ask how those areas are supervised instead, such as open doors or two adults present.

### Are live CCTV feeds for parents a good idea?

They can reassure some parents, especially in the first weeks. But they show other children too, and they can add worry. Ask who can log in and whether recording or sharing clips is allowed.

### Can I ask to see CCTV footage if my child is hurt?

You can ask, and a good centre will have a process for it. They may review it with you rather than hand over a copy, to protect other children's privacy.

# Settling into daycare: how to handle the first two weeks and separation anxiety
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/settling-in-at-daycare/

Daycare separation anxiety is common, and for most children it eases over the first few weeks. A gradual start, a short and predictable goodbye, and steady contact with the teachers help the most. Tears at drop-off usually tell you your child is attached to you, not that the centre is wrong.

The first two weeks are often harder on parents than children. Here's how to get through them.

## Before day one

- **Visit together.** Spend an hour at the centre with your child before the start date. Let them explore while you stay nearby.
- **Talk about it simply.** "You'll play at school, eat lunch, have a nap, and Papa will come after nap time."
- **Practise short separations.** Leave your child with a grandparent or friend for an hour or two in the weeks before.
- **Pick a comfort object.** A small soft toy or a piece of cloth that smells of home. Ask the centre if it's allowed.
- **Share the routine.** Tell teachers about naps, food, words your child uses and what soothes them.

If you're still choosing, our guide on [how to choose a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) covers what to look for, including a settling-in policy.

## A gradual two-week plan

Most good centres suggest a phased start. Here is one common shape. Your centre may suggest something different, and that's fine.

| Days | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 to 2 | One to two hours. You stay in the room or nearby. |
| 3 to 4 | Two to three hours. You leave for a short while, then come back. |
| 5 to 6 | Half day, including one meal. |
| 7 to 8 | Half day with a nap. |
| 9 to 10 | Full day, with an earlier pickup if you can. |

Some children breeze through this in a few days. Others need a week or two longer. Every child is different, so follow your child's pace rather than the calendar.

Plan settling in before you return to work, not on your first day back. Our guide to [childcare after maternity leave](/blog/childcare-after-maternity-leave/) has a full timeline.

## The goodbye routine

How you leave matters more than how long you stay.

1. **Keep it short.** Two or three minutes, once your child is with a teacher.
2. **Keep it the same.** The same words, hug and wave every day. Predictability builds trust.
3. **Always say goodbye.** Slipping away while your child is distracted can make the next drop-off harder.
4. **Tell them when you'll be back,** in terms they understand: "after snack", "after nap".
5. **Leave, even if they cry.** Hand over to the teacher and go. Hovering at the door often makes it longer.

It helps if both parents do drop-off sometimes. Children learn that either parent leaves and comes back. See [dads and daycare](/blog/dads-and-daycare/) for ideas on sharing it.

## What's normal in the first weeks

These are all common while a child adjusts:

- Crying at drop-off, sometimes for a few weeks
- Settling within minutes after you leave
- Being extra clingy, tired or cranky in the evenings
- Eating or napping less at the centre at first
- Sleep changing at home for a while
- Seeming fine for a week, then protesting in week two

That last one surprises many parents. The novelty wears off, and your child realises this is the new routine. It usually passes.

## Talking to teachers

Ask:

- How long did my child cry after I left?
- Did they eat, nap and play?
- Who did they go to for comfort?
- What helped them calm down?
- Is there anything you'd like us to do differently at home?

A good centre will tell you honestly, including the hard parts. Clear daily notes help a lot in these weeks. Here's what daily updates to expect.

## When to talk to someone

Most settling difficulties ease with time. Talk to the centre if, after several weeks, your child:

- Still cries for a long time after drop-off most days
- Doesn't seem to have bonded with any adult at the centre
- Seems very withdrawn, or upset about going in a way that is new

Also trust what you see. If your child is unhappy with a particular adult, or the centre won't share how the day went, take it seriously. Our list of [daycare red flags](/blog/daycare-red-flags/) can help you think it through.

If you're worried about your child's health, sleep or behaviour beyond settling in, speak to your paediatrician. They know your child and can advise you properly.

## Looking after yourself

Leaving a crying child is hard. That's okay.

Ask the teacher to message once your child has settled. Avoid big meetings on the first mornings. Give it two to three weeks before deciding it isn't working.

Kribble will bring photos, updates and teacher notes into one feed, which helps when you want to know how the day went.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long does daycare separation anxiety last?

It varies. Many children settle within two to four weeks, though some take longer. Protests often return briefly after holidays or illness.

### Should I sneak out when my child is distracted?

It's usually better to say a short, clear goodbye. Sneaking out can make your child more anxious about when you might disappear next. A predictable routine builds trust.

### Is it normal for my child to cry every morning at daycare?

Crying at drop-off is common in the first weeks, and many children stop within minutes of you leaving. Ask teachers how quickly your child settles after you leave. If crying continues for a long time each day after several weeks, talk to the centre.

### What is a good settling-in period for daycare?

About two weeks of gradually longer days works for many children, starting with an hour or two while you're nearby. Follow your child's pace and your centre's advice, and plan it before you return to work.


---

# What is the right age for preschool in India?
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/right-age-for-preschool-india/

In India, preschool usually starts at around age 3. That is when the National Education Policy 2020 begins the foundational stage. Many centres also run playgroups for children from about 2. There is no single right age, though: readiness matters as much as the number.

Below is what the policy says, how class names map to ages, and how to tell whether your child is ready.

## What NEP 2020 says about preschool

The National Education Policy 2020 replaces the old 10+2 school structure with a 5+3+3+4 design. The first five years are called the foundational stage, covering ages 3 to 8, according to the [PRS Legislative Research summary of NEP 2020](https://prsindia.org/policy/report-summaries/national-education-policy-2020).

That foundational stage has two parts:

- Three years of preschool, Anganwadi or Balvatika, from about age 3 to 6
- Classes 1 and 2, from about age 6 to 8

The policy also says every child should move into a "Preparatory Class" or "Balavatika" before age 5. That is from the government's [summary of NEP 2020's salient features](https://www.eoibucharest.gov.in/docs/1596447766SalientFeatures.pdf). It describes learning in this stage as play-based and activity-based.

In February 2023, the Ministry of Education asked states and union territories to make six the minimum age for Class 1. [The Tribune reported the advisory](https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/nation/govt-asks-all-states-uts-to-make-6-years-minimum-age-for-class-1-admission-482162). The same report described the aim of giving all children access to three years of quality preschool before that.

Admission ages and cut-off dates are set by states and individual schools. Rules also change. Always check the exact cut-off date with the school you are applying to.

## Typical preschool class names and ages

Indian preschools use a mix of names. If Class 1 starts at 6, the years before it usually work back like this:

| Class name | Usual age at start | What it often looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Playgroup | About 2 | Short sessions, play, songs, first time in a group |
| Nursery (Pre-KG) | About 3 | Routine, language, stories, early motor skills |
| LKG (Lower KG) | About 4 | Early number and letter sounds, group activities |
| UKG (Upper KG) | About 5 | School readiness, longer focus, early reading and counting |
| Class 1 | 6 and above | Formal primary school begins |

These are typical patterns, not rules. Some schools call the year before Class 1 "Balvatika" or "Prep". Others combine years or use their own names. Ask each school which class your child would join, based on their date of birth.

## Signs your child may be ready for preschool

Age is a starting point. These signs often matter more:

- **Can manage short separations.** Your child can stay with a grandparent or friend for an hour or two without lasting distress.
- **Shows interest in other children.** They watch, copy or try to join in with other children at the park.
- **Can follow a simple instruction.** "Put your shoes here" or "come and sit down" mostly works.
- **Communicates basic needs.** With words, signs or gestures, they can show you they are hungry, thirsty or need the toilet.
- **Has some stamina for a routine.** They can manage a morning out without becoming completely exhausted.

Toilet training is not always required. Many preschools help with it, especially for younger groups. Ask each school about its approach.

If your child isn't showing these signs yet, waiting a few months is completely fine. Children develop at different speeds. If you have concerns about your child's development, speak to your paediatrician rather than relying on a preschool's view.

## Starting later: is that a problem?

No. The Ministry of Education's guidance puts Class 1 at 6 and above, and NEP 2020 plans preschool from 3. Starting at 3 rather than 2 fits that design.

What matters more than an early start is what your child does there. Play, talk, stories, music and outdoor time build the foundations. Worksheets and drilling do not. Our guide to what good early learning looks like explains the difference.

## Daycare can start much earlier

Preschool and daycare are different things. Daycare is mainly about care during your working hours, and many daycares take babies.

If you are returning to work, your child may start daycare well before preschool age. Many centres then move children into preschool classes as they grow, often in the same building. Our guide to [preschool vs daycare vs playschool](/blog/preschool-vs-daycare/) explains how these fit together.

## How to choose once you've decided

Once you know the age and type of care, the next step is choosing the right centre. Visit three or four, ask the right questions and, if you can, try a day before you commit.

Our [complete daycare and preschool checklist](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) walks you through each step. Our guide to [preschool approaches](/blog/montessori-vs-playway-vs-reggio/) helps you understand what Montessori, play-way and others mean in practice.

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to compare preschool admissions and daycare plans at centres its team has visited and checked.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the minimum age for preschool in India?

NEP 2020's foundational stage starts at age 3, so that is the age the policy plans preschool around. Many centres also run playgroups from about 2. Check each school's own age rules and cut-off date.

### What age is nursery in India?

Nursery usually starts at about age 3, if Class 1 starts at 6. Schools set their own cut-off dates, and the names vary. Ask the school which class matches your child's date of birth.

### Is 2 years too early for preschool?

Not necessarily. Many children enjoy a short playgroup session at 2. But there is no need to rush. If your child isn't ready to be apart from you yet, starting at 3 is perfectly normal.

### What is Balvatika?

Balvatika is a name used for the preparatory year or years before Class 1. NEP 2020 describes a "Preparatory Class" or "Balavatika" that children join before age 5. Schools use the term in slightly different ways, so check what it means at yours.

# Why you should try a daycare for a day before you enrol
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/trial-day-before-enrolling/

A daycare trial day lets you see how your child, the staff and the routine fit together before you pay admission fees. A visit shows you the building and the manager. A trial day shows you how the centre treats your child on an ordinary day.

If a centre offers a trial, or lets you book a single day, it is worth doing before you commit.

## Why a visit isn't enough

On a visit, you see the centre at its best. Staff know a parent is watching, and you only stay for half an hour or so.

A trial day is closer to real life. You see how staff handle your child's tears, meals, nap and play over several hours. You also see what your child says and does afterwards.

It can save you from a costly mistake. Admission fees and deposits are often non-refundable, so a day's trial is a small step before a large commitment. Our guide to [daycare fees](/blog/daycare-fees-explained/) explains what you might be paying for.

## What to ask before you book

Not every centre offers trial days, and they work differently. Ask:

- Do you offer a trial day, or a short paid day, before enrolment?
- What hours would my child attend?
- Can I stay for part of it, or should I leave?
- Will my child be with the same group and caregiver they would have if they joined?
- Is the trial fee adjusted against admission if we enrol?
- What should I send with my child?

Ask for the trial on a normal weekday, with the usual group. A day with only a few children won't show you much.

## How to prepare your child

A little preparation makes the day easier for everyone.

1. **Talk about it simply.** "Tomorrow you'll go to a new place with toys and other children. I'll come back after lunch."
2. **Visit together first, if you can.** Even ten minutes in the room helps.
3. **Pack familiar things.** A favourite toy, a comfort blanket, a change of clothes and any food your child needs.
4. **Share your child's routine.** Tell staff about nap times, food likes and dislikes, allergies, and how your child is usually comforted.
5. **Keep the goodbye short and warm.** A hug, a clear "I'll be back after lunch" and then leave. Long goodbyes often make it harder.
6. **Keep the day short.** A half day is often enough for a first trial, especially for younger children.

Some tears at drop-off are normal. They don't mean the centre is wrong for your child. Our guide to [settling into daycare](/blog/settling-in-at-daycare/) explains what usually happens in the first weeks.

## What to watch during the trial

If you can stay for part of the day, or watch during drop-off and pickup, look for these.

### How staff greet your child

Does a caregiver come to your child, kneel to their level and say hello by name? A warm first greeting is a good sign.

### How they handle tears

Do staff comfort your child calmly and stay close? Or is your child left to cry while staff carry on? Ask how long the crying lasted after you left.

### Whether your child is included

Is your child invited to join activities, shown where things are and introduced to other children? Or left on the edge?

### Meals and nap

Ask what your child ate and whether they slept. For a first day, little sleep is common. What matters is how staff tried to help.

### How the room runs

Notice whether the day feels calm and organised, or chaotic. Count the adults and children. Our [teacher-to-child ratio guide](/blog/teacher-child-ratio-guide/) explains what to expect at each age.

## What to look for at pickup

Pickup tells you a lot.

- **The handover.** Does a caregiver tell you specific things about the day, such as what your child played, ate and how they slept?
- **Your child's mood.** Tired is normal. Relaxed, chatty or eager to show you something is a great sign.
- **What your child says.** Over the next day, listen for names of teachers or children, and stories about activities.
- **Pickup checks.** Did staff check your identity before handing your child over?

If anything worries you, compare it with our list of [daycare red flags](/blog/daycare-red-flags/).

## After the trial

Write down your impressions that evening. Add them to your notes from the visit. If you have tried more than one centre, a simple [comparison scorecard](/blog/compare-daycares-scorecard/) helps you weigh them up.

Remember that one day is a snapshot. A child who struggled may settle well with a gradual start. A child who loved it may still need a few weeks to adjust. Use the trial alongside everything else in our [complete guide to choosing a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/).

Kribble will offer One-Day Daycare. You'll be able to book verified childcare for a single day, before you enrol or whenever you need backup.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do daycares in India offer trial days?

Some do, and some offer short paid days or allow you to stay with your child for a session. Policies vary, so ask each centre directly. If a centre doesn't offer a trial, ask whether you can spend a morning there with your child.

### How long should a daycare trial day be?

A half day is often enough, especially for babies and toddlers. It gives your child time to experience play and a meal without becoming overwhelmed. You can try a full day later if needed.

### Should I stay with my child during the trial?

It depends on the centre and your child. Staying for the first hour helps you see how staff interact with your child. Leaving for part of the day shows you how your child copes without you.

### What if my child cries the whole trial day?

It doesn't necessarily mean the centre is wrong. Many children need a few weeks to settle. Ask staff how they comforted your child, and consider a gradual start with shorter days.
